title: Conservatives pledge to ban foreign nationals from social housing
description: The Conservatives have said they would end the provision of social housing for foreign nationals in England if they win power at the next election.The
body: The Conservatives have said they would end the provision of social housing for foreign nationals in England if they win power at the next election.The party said ending new tenancies for all foreign nationals, as well as current tenancies for couples where neither person is a UK, Irish or EU citizen, would free up an estimated 228,144 homes for British families.The Conservatives said Labour had "lost control of immigration" and British families had been left sitting on housing waiting lists as a result.But Labour said the policy was an "unserious, unworkable proposal, copied from Reform, that does nothing to tackle the housing crisis the Tories themselves created".In June, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said he would make it a requirement for foreign national tenants to find private accommodation within three months or face possible deportation if his party won power.Under the Tory proposals, ineligible tenants would be expected to move out of their homes within six months. Any single person currently living in social housing who is not a UK, Irish or EU citizen would lose their social home. This includes those with or without children.Couples, where neither of them are UK or EU citizens, and they do not have EU settled status, will also lose their entitlement.Anyone with EU settled status would not be evicted.For future tenancies, UK nationals and those with EU settled status would be eligible but any new EU citizens without settled status would not be.Foreign nationals with settled status, refugee status, or specific humanitarian protections can currently qualify for social housing.Asylum seekers are not eligible for social housing, unless in exceptional circumstances such as domestic abuse cases.Social housing, usually provided by housing associations or local councils, is typically cheaper and more secure than privately rented homes.When they were last in government in 2024, the Conservatives were considering plans to make it a requirement for foreign nationals to have to live in the UK for 10 years before qualifying for social housing. There are 1.34 million households on social housing waiting lists, as of March 2025, the latest government figures.The vast majority of social housing lettings are given to single people. In 2024-25, most lead tenants of new social lettings, the person in whose name the social home is rented, were UK nationals - 89% or 233,000 tenants.In the same period, 2.3% of new lettings were given to refugees - 800 refugees were UK nationals, while the remaining 3,900 were non-UK nationals. The most common nationality of refugees in a new social letting was Afghanistan with the second most common being Ukraine.Conservative shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said: "Making Britain your home should be earned by working, paying tax and integrating."It should not come with a free ride on the benefits system. Britain cannot be a cash machine for the world."Labour has lost control of immigration and lost control of the welfare bill, and it is British families picking up the bill and sitting on waiting lists."Labour said the Conservative policy would primarily affect refugees and long-term UK residents who had contributed to the country, while also leaving more families at risk of homelessness."No amount of headline-chasing, or following Reform to the extremes, can hide the damage the Tories did to our housing system. The least they could do is acknowledge their failures and apologise," the spokesperson said.Housing and homelessness charity Shelter said there were already strict rules on eligibility for social housing and accommodation was not handed out to people on arrival."These divisive plans would brutally kick people out of their homes, including thousands of families and pensioners who have lived in them for decades," chief executive Sarah Elliott said."The housing emergency is caused by successive governments failure to build enough genuinely affordable social homes - not by who accesses social housing."Reform UK's home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf said the Conservatives were trying to copy his party's policy but accused them of not going far enough as their proposed ban does not include those with EU settled status."Incredibly, Kemi Badenoch's new policy is to allow tens of thousands of foreign nationals from the EU to occupy British social housing funded by British taxpayers," he said."Reform UK will ensure British social housing is strictly for British citizens."

schema.headline: Conservatives pledge to ban foreign nationals from social housing

title: Lauryn Hill and Wyclef Jean 'in an amazing place' as fans hope for new Fugees album after 30 years
description: The renewed bond between the two was evident during the interview. When asked about the possibility of a new album, Jean began by restating the questi
body: The renewed bond between the two was evident during the interview. When asked about the possibility of a new album, Jean began by restating the question, "Will there be music in the future?", and Hill chimed in: "Absolutely."Jean continued: "All I can tell you is, man, we're in God's hands,” before singing: “I’m back with my bandmate!"So we're in an amazing place. I think the energy is very important."He suggested they would continue "projecting that love" to the world.Hill added: "There was an incredible healing process that happened with us as a band and as bandmates, and as you said we just want to showcase that and give some of that energy to the world as well."The comments will fuel hopes of a full Fugees reunion, although neither artist confirmed that a new album is currently being recorded.The group's third member, Pras Michel, is currently serving a prison sentence in the United States following his conviction in a federal lobbying and fraud case.Hill and Jean were speaking ahead of Diaspora Calling! By Ms. Lauryn Hill, a one-day festival that will make its UK debut at the Milton Keynes National Bowl on Friday.The event will feature performances from Hill, Jean, Erykah Badu, Giggs, Fireboy DML, YG Marley and Zion Marley, with comedian Dave Chappelle hosting.Reflecting on the anniversary of The Score, Jean said the Fugees' ambitions had always extended beyond music."I remember saying from a very young age, we're not going to do music, we're going to be a movement," he said.He said the themes explored by the group three decades ago remain as relevant as ever."When you talk about the idea of refugees, look where we are today. We were saying these things 30 years ago. It was never just about us – it was always about the movement."Hill said the Fugees themselves embodied the idea behind Diaspora Calling."Our different places of origin came together to unite culture, reflect culture and show people how beautiful, powerful and resourceful that culture is," she said.Earlier in the day, Hill and Jean surprised fans with a pop-up appearance in London's Piccadilly Circus, performing an a cappella rendition of Ready or Not.Hill said London was the natural place to launch the festival."There's so much of the diaspora in London," she said. "So many people are represented here. It felt like a full-circle moment for us."

schema.headline: Lauryn Hill and Wyclef Jean 'in an amazing place' as fans hope for new Fugees album after 30 years

title: Argos is getting a makeover - but can it attract new shoppers?
description: ByDaniel ThomasBBC NewsDo you still shop at Argos? And if so, what do you think of it?The chain has been a fixture of the British High Street for more
body: ByDaniel ThomasBBC NewsDo you still shop at Argos? And if so, what do you think of it?The chain has been a fixture of the British High Street for more than 50 years and is still used by around half of all UK households.But it has struggled to thrive in recent years amid fierce competition from online giants like Amazon, with sales stagnating.  Its owner Sainsbury's recently announced it was selling the chain for a lot less than it paid for it just 10 years ago. But the new owners say they see "real opportunities" for growth, including opening new standalone shops. Can they succeed where Sainsbury's did not?Image caption, Enrico has fond memories of using Argos's now-discontinued print catalogue When the BBC spoke to shoppers in central London this week, the retailer seemed to divide opinion. Some, like Enrico, 28, said they loved the convenience of same-day collection, and felt nostalgic towards a brand which unlocked fond childhood memories."It was a great way of doing your Christmas shopping," he told the BBC. "We'd go into our local Argos and we'd get the massive print catalogue."For others, though, Argos has not moved with the times and is at odds with the seemingly endless online choice. "I feel Amazon is a lot easier because it gets delivered straight to your door with Prime," said Emily, 22, adding that she only used Argos to buy appliances, not "day to day" items.Jack Cunningham, 26, from Kent often uses Argos to pick up things when he's at work in London.The scientist said the big draw was convenience: "If I need something in the moment and can't wait for delivery, normally I'll get it in Argos."You can order something really cheap on Amazon, and it might come and be the wrong size," he added.For years, commentators have asked whether Argos could build a business to take on Amazon, the biggest online seller in the UK.But while Argos has invested a lot in digital, it never quite happened. It made £4.1bn of sales last year, compared with £32bn for Amazon in the UK.'Remind people it exists'Image source, Mike Kemp/In Pictures via Getty ImagesImage caption, Argos has around 200 standalone shops, down from 845 in 2016 Argos does, however, offer something its online rivals don't - a large network of stores, concessions in Sainsbury's shops, and collection points that mean customers can click and collect on the same day, free of charge.Retail analyst Catherine Shuttleworth thinks Argos could capitalise on this, along with its reputation as a trusted British brand. However, she thinks it needs to improve its app so it can compete with online players like Amazon, Shein and Temu.  "I think if you asked people to name five High Street retailers, they wouldn't name Argos," she added. "It's almost about reminding people it exists."Figure caption, What do people want from Argos?Argos hasn't been front of mind for Georgia, 27, for ages. She thinks it is outdated and not for her. "It's very old school isn't it? I'm more of an Amazon shopper."Argos could also do better on customer service, thinks Hugh Radojev, editor of Retail Week.  "It's not an exciting place to shop, or what it used to be for kids around Christmas. Under a new ownership you'd hope they could get it back into the zeitgeist." Image caption, Nicole wants Argos to open more standalone shopsSince 2012, Argos has gone from having 845 standalone shops to around 200 - although it also has opened about 450 shop-within-shops in Sainsbury's stores. This was seen as a smart move, allowing Argos to tap into Sainsbury's large customer base. Argos will keep all of those concessions after the takeover, and customers will continue to get Nectar loyalty card points for all their purchases.But Nicole, 40, an Argos fan from South London, says she wants the chain to expand further."It would be nice if they could go in other supermarkets like Tesco," she added.'Argos has a history of being different'Argos's new owners have ruled out deals with rival supermarkets, but they do plan to forge other "partnerships" and open new standalone stores. The group, called Swift Partners, includes several seasoned retail veterans, one of them a former boss of Co-operative Group. Retail analyst Richard Hyman thinks this ownership will be a better fit than Sainsbury's, which was focused on selling food. But he is sceptical about how much Argos can grow in such a "tough retail market".Shuttleworth is more optimistic, saying with a "ruthless focus" Argos can thrive and even put Amazon under pressure."Argos completely revolutionised the way we shop when they came out and they have a history of being different," she said. "If I was marketing director I would be thinking about how to bottle that for 2027."

schema.headline: Argos is getting a makeover - but can it attract new shoppers?

title: Meta told to pay another $567m in New Mexico child safety lawsuit
description: A US judge in New Mexico on Thursday ordered Meta to pay another $567m (£421m) for its failure to warn the public about dangers its platforms posed to
body: A US judge in New Mexico on Thursday ordered Meta to pay another $567m (£421m) for its failure to warn the public about dangers its platforms posed to children, marking the largest ruling against the company over child safety.Judge Bryan Biedscheid said the social media giant is a "public nuisance" akin to air pollution and that it must put the money in a fund aimed at reducing future harms.  The ruling is in addition to $375m in fines Meta was already ordered to pay in the case, for a total of $942m.Judge Biedscheid compared Meta to a factory, with advertising and content as its product and "the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children to be the pollution that must be abated".A spokesman for Meta, which owns and operates Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp and Threads, said Thursday: "We disagree with the ruling and will appeal.""We work hard to keep people safe on our platforms and have been transparent about the challenges of identifying and removing bad actors and harmful content. We remain confident in our record of protecting teens online and will continue to defend ourselves against claims that misrepresent the facts."Regarding the earlier $375m verdict in the case, Meta had said it intended to appeal the ruling and gave a similar explanation. It was the first time that a state had successfully sued Meta over child safety issues.Meta is currently facing thousands of lawsuits in the US over similar issues. In addition to the New Mexico rulings, Meta earlier this year lost a case in Los Angeles making similar claims.The New Mexico case stems from a 2023 lawsuit brought by attorneys for the State of New Mexico, arguing Meta should be held liable for the way in which its platforms endangered children and exposed them to sexually explicit material and contact with sexual predators.In the first phase of the trial, Meta was found to have repeatedly violated New Mexico's Unfair Practices Act as its recommendation algorithms essentially "steered" young users toward harmful content and contacts.Recommendation algorithms are the tools that Meta uses to automatically curate the content a user sees on its platforms.In ruling on this second phase of the trial, Judge Biedscheid found that Meta's harms reached the level of "public nuisance", or an issue of health and safety that has become so widespread it is negatively impacting a general public.In addition to being the largest fine Meta has received over child safety issues, the ruling also appears to be the first time that a social media company has been deemed a public nuisance."Just as noxious pollution produced by the factory can harm the common public right to reasonably clean air, the harmful effects of Meta's platforms on children do not stay contained by its platforms and, instead, migrate to the internet as a whole and, perhaps most concerning, to the real world and create a common, societal burden on and harm to the affected children and their families and schools, as well as hospitals and law enforcement," the judge wrote.The fund that Meta has been ordered to create will be used to pay for efforts to mitigate "the wide-ranging impacts of the harm", Judge Biedscheid said.A vast majority of the money, totaling $420m, will go towards treatment of harms Meta's platforms have already caused, through the funding of "appropriate clinical or other behavioral health programs and professionals," according to the order.Another chunk of the money will go towards training around awareness and prevention, including for teachers and health professionals on how to deal with social media harms against children.The judge also ordered Meta to enact other measures, including ensuring that no account of a user under age 18 is recommended to an adult and that no adult can message an underage user, banning the sending or receiving of nudity by underage users and enacting a "1-strike policy for adult users who engage in child sexual exploitation."In addition, Meta was ordered to:Eliminate "like" counts for users under 18Ban push notifications for such users every day between 10:00 PM to 7:00 AM and to ban such notifications during the typical school year between  8:00 AM to 3:00 PM, except on weekendsImplement a mandatory usage limit for such users of 90 cumulative hours per month across Instagram and Facebook, or about three hours per dayNext week, another major trial against Meta begins in California. Nearly three dozen US states' attorneys general are suing the company for violating child privacy laws.

schema.headline: Meta told to pay another $567m in New Mexico child safety lawsuit

title: Trump denies US munitions shortage and said he'd seek to jail 'leakers'
description: "Each day, the signs of the enemy's diminishing capabilities become more apparent," Defence Minister Majid Ibn-e-Reza posted on X. "But our Armed Forc
body: "Each day, the signs of the enemy's diminishing capabilities become more apparent," Defence Minister Majid Ibn-e-Reza posted on X. "But our Armed Forces - backed by the nation's defence industry - are fully equipped to respond to any threat."He added that "those who are now seeking to buy security and military superiority through imported systems will soon realise that Iran's indigenous technology is superior to any system in the region".After the US spent vast quantities of difficult-to-manufacture weapons during the combat operation known as Operation Epic Fury and the tit-for-tat strikes since, the Trump administration has sought to assure Americans that the country's missile stockpiles remain robust.CBS News, the BBC's US partner, reported the US has gone through much of its global stockpile of long-range precision missiles during the war, citing two unnamed sources with direct knowledge of the subject.Meanwhile, the Washington Post reported on Wednesday evening that Trump had confronted Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth last week over a possible weapons shortfall, also citing unnamed sources. The BBC has not confirmed the report."The 'leakers' of these treasonous statements are being hunted down," Trump said in the post on Truth Social. "Long term jail sentences will be sought!" He directly addressed the Washington Post's story in a later post, saying: "I really believe their fake 'reporting' is treasonous!" "I am extremely happy with the job that Pete Hegseth is doing," he also posted.Precise information on US missile stocks remains classified. Since becoming secretary, Hegseth has sought to put in place strict controls limiting the information that reporters can gather from the Pentagon, as well.Using publicly available data, the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a national security think tank, estimated that by the end of July, the US had between 759 and 827 Patriot missiles left - about a third of the 2,330 available before the conflict began. It also estimates the US has now used around 60% of terminal high altitude area defense (THAAD) missiles, which are deployed to intercept strikes, Mark Cancian, a retired Marine Corps colonel and senior adviser at CSIS, said on Wednesday.The US is facing demand for its weapons beyond the conflict with Iran, which could also put a strain on supplies.It has given Ukraine significant numbers of Patriot missiles since Russia invaded in 2022, but as US stocks shrink Cancian expects the Pentagon will hold onto them. At a cabinet meeting on Friday, Trump told reporters that granting Ukraine's recent request for additional Patriot missiles would be a "big step", but the two countries were "still talking about" it.Many modern weapons have long funding, order, production, and delivery timelines, making it hard to swiftly replace munitions once they are used.The administration has consistently stated the US has enough in its stockpile. Trump told the Wall Street Journal last month: "We have far more munitions than anyone in the world, and far more than we need."Hegseth, meanwhile, called reports of a stockpile shortage a "manufactured story" on a 14 June appearance on CBS' Face the Nation.But the administration has also indicated it is ramping up production, with Hegseth saying the US was working quickly to manufacture more weapons.Last month, he asked the US Senate for emergency funds totalling $87bn (£68bn) to pay service members and "rapidly replenish equipment and munitions."

schema.headline: Trump denies US munitions shortage and said he'd seek to jail 'leakers'

title: Tour de France Femmes: Kimberley Le Court wins stage six as Marlen Reusser retains yellow jersey
description: Kimberley Le Court overcame a mechanical failure before winning a sprint finish to seal victory in stage six of the Tour de France Femmes on Thursday,
body: Kimberley Le Court overcame a mechanical failure before winning a sprint finish to seal victory in stage six of the Tour de France Femmes on Thursday, as Swiss rider Marlen Reusser held on to the overall lead. Le Court of AG Insurance-Soudal, who also crashed early on in the stage, was forced her to change bike just 15 km from the end. The Mauritian fought her way back into contention shortly before the day's final climb, forming part of a small eight-rider breakaway group 10 km from the finish. Le Court, 30, had just enough performance left to launch a sprint with 300m to go, holding off French rider Cedrine Kerbaol on the line to seal victory, with Puck Pieterse of the Netherlands taking third place.Movistar's Reusser retains the yellow jersey after the 153.4km ride from Montbrison to Tournon-sur-Rhone, holding a 12-second lead over Dutch rider Demi Vollering. title: Artificial Intelligence used to design brand new viruses
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The AI models were trained on genetic codes from viruses, bacteria, plants and peopleByHealth and science cor
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The AI models were trained on genetic codes from viruses, bacteria, plants and peopleByHealth and science correspondentArtificial Intelligence has been used to design brand new viruses that are fully functional and can replicate in the laboratory, say US researchers.It is the first time whole genomes have been successfully designed by AI.The resulting 16 novel viruses were created to infect bacteria and pose no threat to people.The breakthrough has been labelled a "very significant turning point" in science that could unlock a new era for treating disease. But experts have also warned AI-designed viruses raise "urgent" safety and security concerns.AI tools are rapidly advancing and have already been used to design new antibiotics.But that is relatively simple compared with designing a new viable virus from scratch."This is a next step in the complexity that's designable by generative AI, this is the first time generative AI has been used to design a complete genome, it's something that can replicate and have other functions inside cells… this was new territory for us," Brian Hie, assistant professor at Stanford University, told the BBC.The technology works similarly to large language models, like ChatGPT, which predict sequences of text.In this instance the AI models, known as Evo1 and Evo2, predict the language of life rather than words.The AI models were trained on genetic codes from viruses, bacteria, plants and people.They were then refined to produce a type of virus, known as a bacteriophage, which infect only specific species of bacteria.Image source, Stanford UniversityImage caption, Assistant professor Brian Hie, pictured on left with a colleague, said of his work "This was new territory for us".The Stanford researchers picked the most promising 302 AI designs and synthesised them in the lab. Of these, 16 proved effective at killing E. coli bacteria.Samuel King, a PhD student in the lab, said they realised the phage were working in the early hours of the morning. The phage were placed on petri dishes growing a layer of bacteria on them and the scientists waited for signs their new viruses were enjoying the feast."We were starting to see these clear spots and it was just extremely exciting," says King. When the results were shared with the wider team "the room spontaneously burst into applause", Hie recalls.Developing new phage could lead to new ways of treating infections that have become resistant to antibiotics.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Phage therapy is seen as a potential solution to the rising tide of bacterial infections that cannot be treated with antibioticsBut the breakthrough also points to the ability of AI to design new biology that goes beyond the natural world – what is known as synthetic biology.Hie argues this has the potential to "massively improve human health" by developing new drugs and therapies.But concerns have already been raised that the same technology could be used maliciously to create new diseases.In a commentary accompanying the publication in the journal Science, Dr Thomas Inglesby and Dr Moritz Hanke from the Center for Health Security at Johns Hopkins University wrote that the findings raise "urgent biosafety and biosecurity questions".They said it was no longer a question of "whether generative viral genome design will exist" but whether it can be used without "enabling serious harm".For example, they said new viruses with the potential to cause disease "should not be pursued".The researchers themselves took steps to maximise safety. They excluded viruses that could infect complex organisms from the training database, performed the research on phage rather than viruses that infect people and it all took place in a secure laboratory.Hie argues even existing safeguards go a long way towards "ensuring that the technology is used for good".From computers bits to atomsViruses are not alive and it would take another significant leap for AI to generate living organisms.The genetic code of the phage is around 5,400 base pairs (letters) long. The smallest genome of a living cell is around 500,000 base pairs. The human genome is three billion base pairs.Hie says "it would probably be a lot of work, but not impossible" to attempt some simple organisms and they were "definitely interested in working towards" that.Prof Marc Güell, from the synthetic biology lab at Pompeu Fabra University in Spain, said the study was a "very significant turning point" because for the "first time in history, we are beginning to design biology on a computer".He said it "allows us to dream of exciting possibilities for tackling humanity's greatest challenges" such as developing phages to tackle disease, enzymes to treat genetic disorders and antibodies that could be used in immunotherapy.Prof Patrick Cai, chair of synthetic genomics at the Manchester Institute of Biotechnology, said the study was an "important milestone"."The significance extends far beyond phages – it suggests that genome language models are beginning to learn the design principles encoded by evolution, opening the door to AI-assisted genome writing."Image source, Stanford University

schema.headline: Artificial Intelligence used to design brand new viruses

title: Serious questions for Cambridge after professor at centre of plagiarism row resigns
description: The University of Cambridge is facing serious questions about its academic standards and push for diversity after its youngest black professor resigne
body: The University of Cambridge is facing serious questions about its academic standards and push for diversity after its youngest black professor resigned amid allegations of copying other academics' research.Jason Arday's appointment in 2023 was hailed at the time as a progressive moment. Now, Cambridge says it has launched an investigation after "new information" emerged about his academic qualifications and honorary appointments.There are two fundamental questions for the university.Did it fail to adequately check Arday's credentials when appointing him, and did it defend that decision because of an institutional push to position itself as more diverse?For one of the world's leading universities known for academic excellence and globally significant research, this is about its institutional culture and decision-making at the highest level.The biggest reputational risk surrounds the accusations of academic plagiarism now under investigation - and denied by Arday - because they get to the heart of what a university is about.The University of Cambridge uses the common definition of plagiarism as "passing off someone else's work as if it were your own without appropriate acknowledgement".There is no allegation more serious that can be levelled at an academic.One of the fundamental purposes of a research-led university is the creation of knowledge through original thinking, insights and inquiry.The quality of this is the foundation of Cambridge's reputation, and a source of significant funding.Arday did not start his university journey at an elite institution.He has a degree from the University of Surrey in education studies and physical education, a master's from St Mary's University in London, and a PhD in education awarded by Liverpool John Moores University.The reason the PhD has attracted so much attention is because it is the first major piece of original research anyone wanting a career as an academic must complete.Arday's critics claim that his work relied on copying other academics without properly crediting their work from the outset, which he denies.He went on to become an associate professor at Durham University and professor of sociology of education at the University of Glasgow.In other words, there is a line of institutions behind Cambridge now facing similar questions about their appointment processes.The entire higher education system relies on accepting the qualifications awarded by another institution in good faith. Regulation and standards are meant to create a common currency.That has now unravelled with what began as a blog a couple of years ago escalating in recent weeks, with more journalists unpicking aspects of Arday's life story and asking questions.It is at this point Cambridge faces questions about whether it was defending its own reputation as much as an individual academic.Just a couple of weeks ago, the university was briefing journalists that this was a campaign against a black academic, its appointment system was rigorous, and it would be robustly defended.So why might Cambridge have had a blind spot that delayed an investigation which could settle the matter?The university has spent the last decade working to redress the perception that the institution is a bastion of affluent white privilege.Roger Mosey, the former master of the university's Selwyn College, said Arday's academic background was "unconventional" for a Cambridge professor, but that his life story as an autistic man who said he could not read until he was 18 was what had seemingly "made him a compelling candidate".Equality, diversity and inclusion are reasonable goals for a leading university, Mosey wrote in the Times, but risk becoming contentious "when they are baked into inflexible policies and questionable appointment processes".Part of the answer may also lie in how black academics feel in general as part of a tiny minority in the wider university community.In the last academic year, only 75 of Cambridge's 6,180 academics at all levels were identified as black, according to the Higher Education Statistics Authority (HESA).If you look at professors across the UK, 270 are identified as black out of a total of more than 26,000, according to HESA definitions - around 1%.The University and College Union has previously highlighted an ethnicity pay gap and called for it to be redressed. It declined to comment on this case.Both Cambridge and Oxford have faced sustained scrutiny over their whiteness as institutions, with vocal critics over the last 15 years including the MP David Lammy.He extracted data from the universities showing how few offers were made to black students despite the number being awarded top A-Level grades which would potentially qualify them for a place.In 2018, Cambridge said it needed help to attract more talented black students, and unexpectedly the rapper Stormzy answered the call by setting up a scholarship to encourage students to apply.Although the support was for a handful of students, it was a reputational coup for the university - allowing it to position itself as a more open and inclusive institution.Now it will have to balance the potential reputational fall out of the Jason Arday row for its academic credibility, with how that might be perceived by future talented black students and academics.

schema.headline: Serious questions for Cambridge after professor at centre of plagiarism row resigns

title: First OpenAI, now Meta - why do AI hacks keep happening?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByLiv McMahonTechnology reporterOver the last fortnight, reports of AI models going beyond their expected bounds - be that t
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByLiv McMahonTechnology reporterOver the last fortnight, reports of AI models going beyond their expected bounds - be that technically or morally - have been seemingly unavoidable.What started with a trickle - ChatGPT-maker OpenAI admitting their AI had hacked the site Hugging Face - has turned into a flood of groups revealing they had discovered instances of AI going out of control.Claude-maker Anthropic, Meta and the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) have now each reported incidents which seem to paint a worrying picture of a world in which tech going rogue is the norm.In reality, each case offers a window into the risks posed by increasingly capable AI agents - and the importance of testing their limits before they are released to the world.The OpenAI incident has, as Hugging Face's co-founder Thomas Wolf described it, come as a "wake-up call" for the tech industry since it happened at the end of July.It was a big moment which caused big companies to reflect on their own systems - and, in some cases, check they hadn't missed something similarly shocking.Anthropic was the first to act. On Friday, the company found three instances out of thousands where its model Claude had managed to gain access to the internet.Then on Tuesday, the AISI, the UK government agency which evaluates cutting-edge models, then said it had detected a "security incident" during a routine evaluation.It had been testing models by both OpenAI and Anthropic, and found they too tried to carry out cyber-attacks - calling for "scrutiny, transparency, and action".Finally followed Meta, which revealed one of its AI models had inadvertently been allowed to access the internet due to a "misconfiguration" during a third-party test.In disclosing the incident, it is following in the footsteps of those before it.Testing questionsBefore AI models are released to the public, they are put to the test in a series of internal and external evaluations.The aim is to figure out their potential to do good or bad, as well has how they perform in benchmarks measuring their skills.These typically take place in what are known as "sandboxes". These are protected spaces designed to mirror real systems - but with strict guardrails in place.In the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident, the AI attacked the sandbox itself, finding a vulnerability which let it access the internet and "go rogue".Figure caption, Watch: Why is the OpenAI cyber-attack so alarming?Meanwhile the AISI said its own incident, which saw two powerful AI tools create fake human profiles to try and trick people in attempted cyber-attacks, was not down to an issue with the sandbox.Instead, it was due to how it went about its tests. The models it tested were granted access to the internet, and the AISI also disabled in-built filters that would usually block dangerous cyber-attacks."To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour," it said, while noting its unexpected "signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours".Prof Alan Woodward, professor of cyber-security at the University of Surrey, said these cases - while distinct in what happened and why - tell an important story."For 30 years, one rule of software testing held firm: whatever happens in the test environment stays in the test environment," he said. "In the past month, that rule has been broken three times.""One model broke out. One walked through a door left open by mistake. One was deliberately given the keys so testers could measure what it would do."He said these were different causes, but they had the same lesson - "the testing lab is now where the risk lives".He told the BBC that as models become more capable, more must be done to secure the environments where they are tested."Testing an AI agent is less like checking code and more like handling a hazardous material: sealed rooms, constant monitoring of what leaves the building, a rehearsed containment plan," he said."AISI contained its incident within an hour. The next organisation may not."Growing capabilitiesFor those developing AI tools which are designed to take actions on a person's behalf, there is a careful balance to be struck between harnessing their benefits and exposing their risks.The benefit is significant. In theory, we could be able to liberate ourselves of dull, menial tasks, such as replying to emails, going to meetings or managing calendars and diaries, by delegating these to capable bots.The downside is that with great power comes great responsibility, and risk.It's something particularly realised when handing power to tools which are not, like us, able to bring a range of values, context and understanding to decisions we made."Recent incidents of frontier AI models carrying out unsanctioned actions and, in some cases, human-like deceptive behaviour on the open internet are a serious reminder of the risks AI capabilities pose," said Ollie Whitehouse, the National Cyber Security Centre's chief technology officer on Tuesday.Some believe the sheer volume of tasks that will be handled by these tools will mean human oversight might not be enough to contain the problem of models going rogue.But in the meantime, many feel strengthening oversight overall is vital if development continues at its same, frenzied pace.What next?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, AI agents are already becoming a part of our digital lives through services like ChatGPT, OpenClaw and ClaudeIt is unlikely Meta will be the last to emerge with findings of models showing they have, as Prof Woodward puts it, "gone to school" - and learnt our own ways of finding and exploiting gaps in systems.For some, these episodes point to clear security failures on the part of AI companies leading the charge on this game-changing, era-defining tech.For others, they are merely another vehicle for tech firms to hype up their powerful models and compete with rivals. For me, both theories hold some grain of truth.But in rearing their head one after another, these events have nonetheless spurred fears about AI's capabilities and where these are headed as developers forge ahead.And the question inevitably moves to what regulators can and should do next.Michael Birtwistle, associate director at the Ada Lovelace Institute, makes the point that the UK lacks legal incentives for AI firms to prevent systems from developing capabilities which could pose dangers, and that there are no repercussions if testing protocols fail.More broadly, Dr Imogen Stead, AI policy manager at the Centre for Long-Term Resilience, told the BBC that with opportunities to test frontier AI systems narrowing for many, governments should follow the UK in setting up dedicated institutes for testing.Improving third-party evaluations with initiatives such as a "trusted tester scheme" for the most risky types of challenges could also be used to limit adverse impacts, she said.Rather than fear an AI-cyber apocalypse in the meantime, Prof Woodward says, "it's a case of 'keep calm and fix stuff'".Additional reporting by Philippa Wain and Imran Rahman-Jones

schema.headline: First OpenAI, now Meta - why do AI hacks keep happening?

title: Bruno Guimaraes: Jaissle not part of Newcastle captain's Arsenal decision
description: Newcastle United manager Matthias Jaissle says a decision about Bruno Guimaraes' future had already been taken by the time he first met the club's dep
body: Newcastle United manager Matthias Jaissle says a decision about Bruno Guimaraes' future had already been taken by the time he first met the club's departing captain.Arsenal are set to complete their protracted £75m move for the midfielder after a breakthrough in discussions.Jaissle briefly spoke to Guimaraes at the club's training camp in Spain earlier this week, but the 28-year-old went on to bid an emotional farewell to his team-mates and club staff."I met him quickly, but the decision was already made," Jaissle said in his first meeting with reporters following his appointment as head coach."It was a nice conversation. He's a fantastic player and a great human being. It's tough but for him now it's the next challenge and we need to deal with it at a later stage. "We trust the players who are here already, but we will also see some changes."Guimaraes is set to become the fourth key player to leave Newcastle in less than a year.Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali moved to Barcelona and Tottenham Hotspur respectively earlier in the window while Alexander Isak joined Liverpool last summer.Club legend Alan Shearer has sent Jaissle his "very best wishes", but previously warned it could be a "tough season" with some "very challenging times ahead" in a column for BBC Sport.Jaissle, though, sees the club's rebuild as an opportunity to start a new cycle and mould a young, hungry side after succeeding predecessor Eddie Howe."This is a challenge and there are so many transitions at the moment," he said. "Many big players left - legends of the club - but we need to see it as a chance."Not having too many excuses now, just thinking forward about what we can influence. "Control the controllables, I used to say, and I'm sure there will be progress this season."Jaissle has been focused on coaching the players currently at his disposal on the training pitches, but Newcastle are working on further additions before the start of the season.Newcastle have shifted policy this summer, targeting younger players on the Continent, with Lukas Hornicek the club's oldest arrival by a reasonable distance at 24 years of age.The club have spent around £146m to date on goalkeepers Hornicek and Ewen Jaouen, midfielders Aladji Bamba and Sean Steur and winger Bazoumana Toure.The quintet, like Jaissle, have never experienced life in the Premier League before.However, following trophy-laden spells in Saudi Arabia and Austria with Al-Ahli and RB Salzburg, the 38-year-old is relishing the challenge ahead."This is something I don't have on my CV, but that's normal in football," he said."At one point it has to be your first step and I'm now at that moment after being successful in Saudi Arabia and Austria. "Everyone was dreaming about being a part of the Premier League and now here we are."Newcastle start the new campaign against Liverpool at St James' Park on 23 August.

schema.headline: Bruno Guimaraes: Jaissle not part of Newcastle captain's Arsenal decision

title: Leeds United transfer news: James Trafford joins from Manchester City in deal worth up to £45m
description: More than £80m has now been spent on Trafford in initial transfer fees.As part of the deal taking him to Leeds, BBC Sport understands City will retain
body: More than £80m has now been spent on Trafford in initial transfer fees.As part of the deal taking him to Leeds, BBC Sport understands City will retain a 20% sell-on clause and have matching rights - meaning if they match a future offer for Trafford they will get first refusal on him.Leeds boss Daniel Farke appears willing to pay a premium despite Trafford's limited opportunities at Manchester City last season, after both Karl Darlow and Illan Meslier left Elland Road this summer.Lucas Perri and Alex Cairns remain on the books, though Perri lost his place to Darlow in the second half of last season and did not feature in the Premier League after a 4-3 defeat by Newcastle on 7 January.Leeds are investing in the potential of a young goalkeeper whose highlights have largely come in the Championship with Burnley, where he conceded just 16 goals in 45 appearances.Trafford has only played 32 top-flight games, but former Clarets boss Scott Parker previously praised his turnaround at Turf Moor before moving to the Etihad.Praised as "world class" by Parker, Trafford's 29 clean sheets and 84.47% save ratio were key to Burnley's promotion back to the Premier League in 2024-25.Trafford began his career at City and had loan spells with Accrington Stanley and Bolton Wanderers before joining Burnley in 2023.He made 73 appearances for the Clarets before City activated their buy-back option last summer.

schema.headline: Leeds United transfer news: James Trafford joins from Manchester City in deal worth up to £45m

title: Old habits haunt Rangers in early McInnes tenure
description: Two games, no wins, and a whole lot of work yet to do - there has been no dream start for Derek McInnes in his dream job.Rangers' 2-1 first-leg defeat
body: Two games, no wins, and a whole lot of work yet to do - there has been no dream start for Derek McInnes in his dream job.Rangers' 2-1 first-leg defeat in their Europa League third-round qualifier away to Jagiellonia Bialystok came hot on the heels of a meek draw at Dundee United in their Scottish Premiership curtain-raiser.McInnes' appointment, many fans hoped, would be a fresh start for the club after a succession of managers who arrived with glowing reviews and bags of promise, before they all left under a cloud of criticism and disappointment. Nine signings have arrived this summer, with more expected, but last year's ruinous form is casting a long shadow."We've seen a lot tonight of what I thought Rangers were last season," McInnes said after the defeat in Poland.It's a damning indictment from someone who knows how high the standards should be at Ibrox.Neither Russell Martin nor Danny Rohl were able to restore past glories in their short stints in Govan while McInnes was taking Hearts to the verge of immortality.Much of the condemnation surrounding the Ibrox club's failures last season came back to the same theme - they may be fluid and clinical going forward at times, but a soft underbelly put paid to hopes of success."I thought we gave up too many chances and gave teams too much encouragement," the 55-year-old added post match in Poland."We've got to be honest and say we are guilty of beating ourselves tonight. And that's no disrespect to our opponent because on transitions and counter-attack, it fuels them."Rangers were flailing in the opening 45 minutes as Jagiellonia cut them open with ease, capitalising on numerous lapses in concentration.Twelve minutes into the game, Thelo Aasgaard tried an audacious spin on the edge of the hosts' box, attempting to squeeze the ball through a small gap in the defence.One minute later it was in the back of Rangers' net following an impressive counter."There's no bigger drain on confidence for any player, team, support than losing cheap goals," McInnes said."There were mistakes for the goals, and I understand that can happen, but we have got to be far more stingy with our work, defend the goal with our lives, don't give our opponent opportunities. "At no cost is that ball going in our box, at no cost are they going to get a chance, and we've got to have a bit more of that approach to our work."The central defensive partnership of Dujon Sterling and Emmanuel Fernandez looked particularly shaky."If you spoke to McInnes right now without a microphone in front of him, and you asked him, 'Do you trust Fernandez?', there's no way he says yes, no way," former Rangers midfielder Andy Halliday said on BBC Sportsound."But he doesn't have an option at this moment in time to play someone else."I'm being very critical here, but I think Fernandez has every attribute to be a top, top central defender, yet it looks as if he hasn't had the education growing up of the basics of being a central defender."Cammy Devlin, Findlay Curtis and Nicolas Raskin were introduced in a triple half-time change and they all played their part in a much better second-half showing from McInnes' side.Curtis was the standout. The 20-year-old was a revelation on loan at Kilmarnock in the second half of last season, earning a call-up to Scotland's World Cup squad.For a Rangers side crying out for attacking guile and inventiveness on the flanks, Curtis being limited to just eight minutes in their Premiership opener against United was surprising.His 45 minutes in Poland - where he struck the post late on and flashed an effort just wide - surely will lead to greater involvement in a team short of attacking impetus right now."The second-half performance was better, in an attacking sense. Findlay Curtis had a large part to play in that," former Rangers striker Steven Thompson said on BBC Sportsound."He didn't have that first thought of, when he received the ball, laying it back or looking for a sitting midfielder."He wants to go and take people on. It's brilliant to see that, because there's not enough of that in this Rangers side. He put in a number of good deliveries."His performance was one of the major positives from the evening."Halliday was similarly impressed, saying: "Curtis had a fearless nature to try to make a positive impact."Not everything came off, but when he gets the ball, he drives at players, he plays one-two, he's running off the ball and having efforts at goal."That alone sparked Rangers into that 5% or 10% more on the ball."

schema.headline: Old habits haunt Rangers in early McInnes tenure

title: Gianni Infantino: Uefa says Fifa's backing of its president 'changes nothing'
description: European teams could still boycott competitions including the World Cup as Uefa says Fifa's defence of its president Gianni Infantino "changes nothing
body: European teams could still boycott competitions including the World Cup as Uefa says Fifa's defence of its president Gianni Infantino "changes nothing".The English FA has sent a letter withdrawing its support for Infantino in reaction to the plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.European governing body Uefa said in a statement its conditions had not been met, despite Infantino's plan being aborted."First, the proposals to sell off the major competitions had to be withdrawn and secondly," Uefa's statement said. "Assurances have to be made that such attempts to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again."These conditions have not been met."Uefa has already said it has lost confidence in Infantino, calling the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal a "shabby, back room, opaque deal".Infantino had offered all associations $40m (£30m) if they backed a proposal for private investment in its tournaments, including the men's and women's World Cups, through the FFE subsidiary.World governing body Fifa said during Wednesday's meeting "mistakes" regarding FFE were "acknowledged", saying it was "not the intention" for the Fifa Council and members association to "feel excluded from the process and that the process should have been handled differently".Uefa's statement in response added: "Uefa made it abundantly clear in its statement on Saturday that it has lost confidence in Gianni Infantino's presidency. That position holds."Yesterday's announcement that some people employed by the Fifa president (and whose careers depend on his favour) agree with him changes nothing."Fifa has been approached for comment.Infantino arrived at Fifa's offices in Rabat, Morocco on Wednesday in now-familiar fashion, chauffeured to the building in a motorcade, sitting in the back of a Mercedes with blacked out windows.Some questioned whether he would still be the Fifa president when he left.Yet if anything, on the surface at least, Infantino appears emboldened.This was not the 56-year-old being ordered to a hearing to explain his actions. It was Infantino who summoned members of the Fifa management board to sit around the table with him, to talk through the events of the last week.Secretary general Mattias Grafstrom, Infantino's right-hand man, had been critical in an internal memo to staff, calling the FFE proposals "a sad and reproachable series of events".After the meeting finished it appeared to be water under the bridge, with Infantino and Grafstrom pictured sat next to each other and smiling at a Women's Africa Cup of Nations match between Malawi and Zambia. If there were clear-the-air talks, they appear to have worked. Other members of the Fifa management board to attend the meeting included finance chief Thomas Peyer, legal chief Emilio Garcia Silvero, chief of staff Daniel O'Toole, chief of member associations Elkhan Mammadov and media relations director Bryan Swanson.BBC Sport has been told that Fifa's chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, was not invited.Lamour strongly criticised Infantino's FFE plan, saying it was "the project of one person", and "the time has now come for football's political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions". He added: "I lose my job, then so be it. At least I'll sleep well tonight."Lamour has declined to comment to the BBC. Fifa has been approached for comment.What concerns Uefa is that this meeting was a gathering of employees who are themselves part of the regime. It is unknown if Infantino was forced to answer difficult questions about his plan. Questions such as: who was involved? Whether there was a competitive tender process? And if he stood to benefit personally? While Fifa said "mistakes made were acknowledged" and an "apology was made", there was no direct accountability for the controversy.Uefa still wants answers to those key questions and will not be content until it gets them - or Infantino leaves.Uefa is in something of a pickle as it tries to get rid of Infantino.The easiest route to success was the slow turning of the vice throughout this week, hoping to exert enough pressure to force him to quit.Yet the Swiss appears to have no intention of walking away.European football looks like an outlier, struggling to gain enough support to topple him. On Thursday, Lamin Kaba Bajo, the president of the Gambia Football Federation, praised Infantino's "courage" and for the U-turn, and said he was "willing to give him my support more than ever".Only Jordan, one of the few countries which did not back Infantino before last week, has publicly stated it will not vote for his re-election in March. Concacaf, which oversees football in North and Central America and the Caribbean, also issued a public statement after the proposal was aborted but, unlike Uefa, it did not go as far as to say it had lost confidence in the Fifa president. Conmebol, the South American confederation, said on Thursday it would not support "any action or procedure that disregards" Fifa's mechanisms before the presidential election. Similarly, the Mexican Football Federation shared a statement to X expressing their support for Infantino, saying it would not recognise or approve any process convened outside of Fifa's institutional framework. The Argentine Football Association also published a letter in support of Infantino and the Fifa board, which it said had provided "institutional solidity" with its current "stable and transparent" business model.The Confederation of African Football (Caf) said its executive committee "unanimously reconfirmed" its support for Infantino and thanked him for his support for African football over the years.Ideally, Uefa would force an emergency meeting of the Fifa Council, to provide what it would consider to be a true chance to hold Infantino to account.But getting the necessary 19 of 36 confederation and football association heads to support it has proven to be exceptionally difficult. Uefa has also kept on the table the option of a vote of no confidence, which it can trigger via an extraordinary congress any time it wishes. However, it would need a majority of Fifa's 211 member associations - 106 votes - to pass the motion. It would be a de facto presidential election without a second candidate. If Uefa does not think it can get to 106, which looks a stretch, then there is little point in triggering the vote. The other option is to try to find a unity candidate to stand against Infantino in the election next March. The favourite would be Concacaf president Victor Montagliani. Any option which takes time gives Infantino space to build bridges, and with Fifa due to announce new funding to member associations by the end of the year he could dangle another carrot for his re-election.  Unless Uefa sticks by the nuclear option - and goes through with its threat of a boycott.This has issues, and it is not a lever you can pull very often, otherwise it gives the impression of riding roughshod over the rest of the world.It is one thing to use it to jettison the FFE proposal, another entirely to effectively dethrone the president with it. Uefa's stance will soon be tested, with the Fifa Women's U20s World Cup kicking off in Poland on 5 September. Six European countries are due to take part, including England. Some at the European confederation claim Wednesday's statement shows exactly why the beleaguered president must step down.The feeling within Uefa is that the statement was far from representative of the entire world governing body, and that there has been a lack of consultation with the council or membership.There is also a view that Infantino is trying to swerve personal responsibility by sharing out the blame for the aborted proposals, and that he alone should have apologised - rather than issue his expression of regret alongside his deputy Grafstrom.In stark contrast, within Fifa, the view from one Infantino loyalist is that the outcry, especially in Europe, is bordering on "hysteria", and fails to acknowledge the legitimacy he has globally.By clinging to power, Infantino has mounted the start of an attempted fightback. But it could yet fuel the revolt against him, both from outside and within Fifa. And it looks increasingly likely his opponents will have to identity the rival candidate that could challenge him at next year's presidential election.

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino: Uefa says Fifa's backing of its president 'changes nothing'

title: Further arrests in Thetford as disorder continues for third night
description: Image source, John Fairhall/BBCImage caption, Police make an arrest in Thetford on Thursday night as the market town braced itself for a third night o
body: Image source, John Fairhall/BBCImage caption, Police make an arrest in Thetford on Thursday night as the market town braced itself for a third night of unrestByNeve Gordon-Farleigh & Orla MooreUpdated 4 hours agoMore arrests have been made in Thetford as disorder linked to anti-immigration protests continued for a third night in the Norfolk market town.A further two men in their 40s were arrested on Thursday evening, Norfolk Police said, taking the total number of people arrested in relation to the disorder to five.One of the pair was arrested on suspicion of racial hatred, relating to offences on Wednesday, the force said. The other man was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly and failing to give his details to police when asked. Policing powers were stepped up in Thetford on Thursday evening following the disorder earlier in the week.It came after police officers were "subjected to significant aggression" on Wednesday, including a female police officer who was "seriously bitten".Crowds also attempted to storm homes linked to alleged asylum seekers on Tuesday and Wednesday evenings. Police removed some people from a property on Thursday evening.Amid the disorder, pictures appeared to show a heavy police presence in the residential area of Canterbury Way on Thursday night.A Home Office spokesperson condemned the behaviour, warning that "anyone taking part in this criminal activity will face the full force of the law".Norfolk Police has imposed public safety measures in the town, including requiring people to remove face coverings if asked to do so or face arrest.They will also be permitted to direct anyone committing, or who they suspect may commit, anti-social behaviour, to leave the area.The measures were put in place from 18:00 BST on Thursday and remain until 07:00 on Friday.Image source, John Fairhall/BBCImage caption, Dozens of police officers have arrived in Thetford for a third night as anti-immigration protests continueTwo police officers were injured in the second night of disorder on Wednesday, with the force confirming that "significant police resources" were deployed as a result.Witnesses reported a crowd of more than 200 people on Clover Way, with eggs and rocks thrown at houses and chants of "we want them out".The force said members of the group "became physically aggressive towards officers – a male officer was struck with a rock and a female officer was seriously bitten, breaking the skin."Assistant chief constable Julie Dean, said: "We will not stand by and allow violence to take place, whether that is directed towards members of the public, local residents or police officers carrying out their duties."A spokesperson for the Home Office said: "The right to protest is fundamental to our democracy and the concerns of communities are central to our immigration reforms."However violence and disorder are never acceptable, and we absolutely condemn the behaviour seen in Thetford, including attacks against frontline police officers."The attacks on officers followed unrest on Tuesday in St John's Way, Bracken Road and Elm Road, when properties were damaged with windows smashed and fences broken, and people attempted to break into a residential property, police said.The Labour MP for South West Norfolk, Terry Jermy, also said the "ugly scenes in Thetford over the past few days have been difficult to watch and are deeply concerning".Image source, John Fairhall/BBCImage caption, People have gathered in Thetford for a third nightImage source, Scott HusseyImage caption, Norfolk Police attended unrest at three addresses in Thetford on Tuesday and the disorder continued the following nightA man in his 30s was arrested on suspicion of a public order offence on Wednesday afternoon following Tuesday's disorder. He was released and issued with a conditional caution.In the early hours of Thursday, two further arrests were made following Wednesday's unrest. One man aged in his 40s remains in custody, and a 68-year-old man from Thetford has been charged with possession of an offensive weapon, namely a wooden bat.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, A large group stormed three properties including this one on Bracken Road, which protesters believed was being used to house asylum seekersACC Dean promised "robust action" to the disorder, adding: "We will always facilitate and support the right to peaceful protest, and we recognise that people may hold strong views and feelings about issues."Our role is to keep people safe. We have a duty to protect everyone in our communities, maintain public order and prevent harm. We will not stand by and allow violence to take place, whether that is directed towards members of the public, local residents or police officers carrying out their duties."Witnesses also claimed the police response on Wednesday was "heavy-handed" and a woman on a mobility scooter had been pepper-sprayed.In response, the police said Pava spray was "deployed proportionately" in response to a person's behaviour in the crowd.A spokeswoman added: "We understand that concerns have been raised about a woman using a mobility scooter who was affected during the incident."It was not the intention for any bystander to be impacted, however, where people remain within an area of active disorder and do not follow police instructions to move away, there is a risk they may be affected by tactics deployed to protect public safety."Image source, John Fairhall/BBCImage caption, The South West Norfolk MP Terry Jermy said "mob rule and vigilantism is not acceptable"Scott Hussey, a Reform councillor for the nearby Brecks division on Norfolk County Council, said a "peaceful protest" had started at the town's police station on Wednesday night before it moved to Clover Way. "I counted up to the 30 officers lined up on one side of the street and on the other side maybe up to 100 protesters," he said."There were some skirmishes, it was a spirited protest but I didn't see any violence."He accused the Home Office of "opening a number of these HMOs across Thetford" and "trying to rush through the site for asylum seekers at Barnham"."We fully support their right to protest. I'd encourage people to protest peacefully and most of what I saw yesterday was peaceful."Jermy has previously called on the Home Office to end "secrecy and confusion" around plans to house more asylum seekers in former military barracks – including at RAF Barnham, near Thetford.In a statement he condemned the unrest, saying: "People have been pulled from their homes – a place of safety – and forcibly removed, with reports of members of the public breaking into homes, taking property and smashing windows."This would have been utterly terrifying for the people in these properties and also very worrying for neighbouring residents."I do not know the immigration status of the people placed in these properties or their legal status, but I know they are human beings that must be afforded the same rights that we all expect in this country."Whatever our own individuals views on immigration - mob rule and vigilantism is not acceptable."Do you have a story suggestion for Norfolk? Contact us below.Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: Further arrests in Thetford as disorder continues for third night

title: How a diary solved the disappearance and murder of Richard Dyson
description: When Det Con Tom Ryan came across a diary entry about an old cattle trailer in July 2025, he knew he had finally solved the murder of a man who had di
body: When Det Con Tom Ryan came across a diary entry about an old cattle trailer in July 2025, he knew he had finally solved the murder of a man who had disappeared six years earlier.Richard Dyson vanished without trace in November 2019. He was last seen alive on 17 November that year and was reported missing eight days later when he failed to meet his daughter, Bethany."He was by all accounts a very good father, and he was regularly in contact with his daughter Bethany who was, I believe, 19 at the time of his disappearance. It was totally out of character," Ryan recalled."It was clear that he had disappeared off the face of the Earth."Richard, who was 55 at the time, had been living in his car at Parkside Cottage on Christopher Wright's farm on Sheffield Road in Barnsley, helping with small jobs around the farm.The farm was searched, but other than a collection of illegal weapons belonging to Wright, nothing more unusual was found and there was no sign of Richard.His phone, however, showed it had never left the farm.Police believed from the outset that Richard had been killed and that Wright and his childhood friend, Karl Schwalbe, were responsible, according to Ryan."We very much suspected their involvement, but without a body it's very difficult to prove murder," he said.On 28 July Wright, 73, and Schwalbe, 72, were convicted for their roles in Richard's disappearance and murder, ending a six-year wait for answers for Richard's family. At a sentencing hearing at Sheffield Crown Court on Thursday, Wright was jailed for 35 years for murder and Schwalbe was given a three-year sentence for perverting the course of justice.But how did police finally catch them?Nearly six years had passed when Ryan reviewed phone records relevant to the case. Among several calls made by Wright, one to Ian Ollerenshaw on 20 November 2019 caught his attention."I went round to Ian's house and I asked him, 'Can you by any way remember that phone call that you received over six years ago' - and, to be entirely honest, I expected him to say no," he said.But the farmer, who lives at Alderthwaite Farm, just over a mile from Parkside Cottage, did remember.More remarkably, he produced a leather diary from 2019, in which he had noted that Wright had stopped by to drop off an old trailer."As soon as I spoke to Ian and he remembered the phone call and he said 'the trailer is still here, do you want to go and see it' - as soon as he said that, I knew I'd found Richard," said Det Con Ryan.The farmer told him the trailer had been sitting padlocked and undisturbed in the corner of a field for years. By the time Det Con Ryan came across it, it was partially obscured by overgrown hedges and long grass.CCTV footage of Richard's last movements on 17 November 2019 further supported what officers already knew - Wright had been the last person to see him alive.The cameras captured Richard returning to Wright's farm shortly after 23:00 GMT.About 20 minutes later, Wright called his friend, Schwalbe. The first call went unanswered, but minutes later a second call, lasting only a few seconds, connected.Not long after, footage showed Schwalbe's car making its way towards Wright's farm."The extent of the physical assistance that Schwalbe provided to Wright is unknown to everybody other than the two men," said Ryan."What is known is that Schwalbe could on any day in the last seven years have helped stop the suffering of Richard's family, but he chose not to."Three days after Richard's disappearance, bank transactions showed Wright went to Allendale Building Supplies in Hoyland. While it was never proved, it was suggested he went there to buy cement.Long before Wright's and Schwalbe's trial began, prosecutors expected Wright to argue that someone else must have been responsible for Richard's disappearance and murder.But senior crown prosecutor Jamie Barton said the investigation consistently pointed in one direction."All lines led to Mr Wright and Mr Schwalbe," she said.However, she said the six-year gap between Richard's disappearance and the discovery of his body left investigators with limited forensic evidence, poorer-quality CCTV than would be expected today and little mobile phone data.Even the murder weapon remained elusive, with none of the weapons seized presenting a link to Richard's fatal injuries.Although prosecutors did not have to prove motive, Barton said detectives uncovered evidence supporting long-standing rumours that Richard had stolen from Wright and, therefore, Wright killed him."It's a case theory, it's not something that we can be certain of - but it's one thing that is relevant," she said.

schema.headline: How a diary solved the disappearance and murder of Richard Dyson
